title: Common Medical Conditions: Epilepsy & Sudden Cardiac Arrest
description: Causes, symptoms and treatment of epilepsy and sudden cardiac arrest, including AED use, CPR and cardiac arrest vs.
content_html:
Two Serious Conditions in Sport

Epilepsy and sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) are two of the most serious medical conditions a coach or sports practitioner may encounter. Both can be life-threatening in a sporting context. Understanding the causes, recognising the symptoms and knowing the correct response can make the difference between life and death. This lesson covers both conditions in the depth required by the specification.

Epilepsy: Overview and Causes

Epilepsy is a neurological condition in which abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain cause recurrent seizures. Not all seizures are the dramatic convulsions often associated with epilepsy — they range from brief lapses in consciousness to full body shaking. Three key triggers are listed in the specification: severe head injuries (which can damage brain tissue and disrupt normal electrical patterns), anxiety or stress (psychological states that can lower the seizure threshold in susceptible individuals) and tiredness or lack of sleep (fatigue reduces the brain's resilience to abnormal electrical activity). In sport, these triggers are all plausible — contact sport carries head injury risk, competition brings stress, and overtrained athletes may be sleep-deprived.

Epilepsy: Symptoms of Seizures

Seizure symptoms affect different parts of the body. In the eyes, a performer may stare blankly or show flickering/fluttering of the eyelids — this may look like a brief lapse of attention or a temporary absence. In the mouth, symptoms include biting the tongue, making random involuntary noises or vocalisation, or producing excessive saliva. In the limbs, seizures may cause stiffness (tonic phase) followed by rhythmic jerking movements of the arms and legs (clonic phase), or sudden loss of muscle tone causing the performer to collapse to the ground.

Key Fact

Epilepsy seizure symptoms affect: eyes (staring blankly, fluttering), mouth (biting tongue, random noises) and limbs (stiffness and jerking movements). The three main triggers in sport are severe head injuries, anxiety/stress and tiredness/lack of sleep.

Epilepsy: Treatment

The two main treatments for epilepsy are anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) — medication taken regularly to reduce the frequency and severity of seizures by stabilising the brain's electrical activity — and the ketogenic diet, a high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet that has been shown to reduce seizure frequency in some patients, particularly children, when medication is not fully effective. In a sporting context, if a performer has a seizure, the immediate response is to protect them from injury (move hard objects away, cushion the head), do not restrain them, place them in the recovery position once convulsions stop, stay with them and call 999 if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or they do not regain consciousness.

A performer with epilepsy should inform their coach and ensure the coaching team know their seizure plan. Sports that involve heights, open water or fast-moving equipment carry additional risk and may require adapted supervision or individual risk assessments. During a seizure, never put anything in the performer's mouth (contrary to myth, swallowing the tongue is not possible). Head protection and the avoidance of severe head trauma are important preventive measures given the link between head injury and seizure triggers.

Sudden Cardiac Arrest: Overview and Causes

Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) occurs when the heart's electrical system malfunctions, causing it to stop pumping blood. Without immediate treatment, brain damage begins within 4–6 minutes and death within 10 minutes. Three causes are listed in the specification: underlying genetic heart conditions — such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), an inherited thickening of the heart muscle that is the most common cause of SCA in young athletes; intense physical activity — which can trigger SCA in those with undetected heart conditions by placing extreme demand on an already abnormal heart; and sudden trauma — a severe blow to the chest at a specific moment in the cardiac cycle (called commotio cordis) can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

SCA vs Heart Attack: A Critical Distinction

The specification requires you to know the difference between cardiac arrest and a heart attack. A heart attack (myocardial infarction) is caused by a blockage in a coronary artery — the heart muscle is starved of blood but continues to beat. The performer is typically conscious, may experience crushing chest pain, breathlessness and pain radiating to the arm or jaw, and can often speak. A sudden cardiac arrest is an electrical failure — the heart stops beating effectively. The performer is unconscious and not breathing normally. Both are emergencies requiring 999, but SCA additionally requires immediate CPR and defibrillation to have any chance of survival.

Key Fact

Sudden cardiac arrest: the heart stops beating (unconscious, not breathing normally) — requires CPR and a defibrillator immediately. Heart attack: a blocked coronary artery starves heart muscle of blood but the heart keeps beating — the performer is conscious. Both require 999 but only SCA requires CPR and defibrillation.

SCA Treatment: CPR and Defibrillation

The symptoms of SCA are: unconsciousness (sudden collapse with no response) and breathing difficulties (agonal breathing — irregular gasping — or complete absence of breathing). Treatment follows the DRABC protocol. Once SCA is suspected, call 999 immediately and begin CPR — 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths, at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute, pushing down 5–6 cm on the centre of the chest. A defibrillator (AED) should be retrieved and used as soon as possible — the AED analyses the heart rhythm and delivers a controlled electric shock if ventricular fibrillation is detected, which can restore a normal rhythm. Every minute without defibrillation reduces survival chances by approximately 10%. Lifestyle changes — including maintaining a healthy weight, not smoking, and regular cardiovascular exercise — reduce the long-term risk of cardiac events.

In the epilepsy section, the specification abbreviates anti-epileptic drugs as 'AEDs'. In the cardiac arrest section, 'AED' means Automated External Defibrillator. These are two completely different things. In an exam, always write the full term first — 'anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs)' or 'Automated External Defibrillator (AED)' — and then use the abbreviation, so the examiner can be certain which you mean. Confusing the two would result in a medically incorrect answer and lost marks.
exam_tip_html: For epilepsy questions, use the specification's exact body-area framework for symptoms: eyes, mouth, limbs — then give one example for each. For SCA questions, be precise about the treatment sequence: call 999, begin CPR (30:2), retrieve and use AED. Do not say 'give CPR' without specifying the compression-to-breath ratio. Always state the key distinction: in cardiac arrest the performer is unconscious and not breathing; in a heart attack they are conscious. This distinction is worth at least 1 mark in any comparison question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Epilepsy seizures are triggered by severe head injuries, anxiety/stress and tiredness; symptoms affect the eyes (staring, fluttering), mouth (biting tongue, random noises) and limbs (stiffness and jerking); treatment is anti-epileptic drugs or a ketogenic diet.
  • Sudden cardiac arrest occurs when the heart stops beating, causing unconsciousness and abnormal or absent breathing; it must be distinguished from a heart attack, where the heart still beats and the performer remains conscious.
  • Treatment for SCA requires immediate 999 call, CPR (30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths) and an AED (Automated External Defibrillator) as soon as possible; every minute without defibrillation reduces survival odds by approximately 10%.

glossary_terms.definition: A neurological condition characterised by recurring seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
Episodes of uncontrolled electrical activity in the brain that temporarily affect movement, sensation, consciousness or behaviour.
A medical emergency where the heart suddenly stops beating effectively, causing loss of consciousness and cessation of normal breathing.
An Automated External Defibrillator: a portable device that delivers an electric shock to restore normal heart rhythm during cardiac arrest.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a symptom of sudden cardiac arrest?
A) Crushing chest pain with the performer still conscious
B) Staring blankly and fluttering eyelids
C) Unconsciousness and breathing difficulties
D) Wheezing and tightness in the chest
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconsciousness and breathing difficulties [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two triggers for an epileptic seizure that are relevant in a sporting context.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: severe head injuries / anxiety or stress / tiredness or lack of sleep. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a heart attack and sudden cardiac arrest.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic distinction (1 mark): in a heart attack the heart keeps beating; in cardiac arrest it stops. Development of heart attack (1 mark): a heart attack is caused by a blockage in a coronary artery that stops blood reaching part of the heart muscle — the performer is typically conscious and may feel crushing chest pain. Development of cardiac arrest (1 mark): sudden cardiac arrest is an electrical failure of the heart — the heart stops pumping effectively, the performer is unconscious and not breathing normally. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a first aider should treat a young athlete who collapses during a race and is suspected to be in sudden cardiac arrest. Give an example of how the AED would be used.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks. Call 999 immediately (1 mark). Begin CPR — 30 chest compressions (5–6 cm deep, centre of chest) to 2 rescue breaths, at 100–120 compressions per minute (1 mark). Retrieve the AED as soon as possible and switch it on (1 mark). AED example (1 mark): the AED gives voice instructions — attach the pads to the bare chest as shown, stand clear while it analyses the heart rhythm, and deliver the shock if prompted; resume CPR immediately after the shock and continue until paramedics arrive. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A swimming club coach is concerned about the risk of medical emergencies during competitive galas attended by up to 200 spectators and 80 swimmers.

Discuss the measures the club should take to manage the risk of epileptic seizures and sudden cardiac arrest during competitive events.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion of measures for both conditions. For epilepsy: pre-event disclosure of seizure plans, adapted supervision near water, designated first aider who knows the protocol, what to do during a seizure (do not restrain, protect from injury, recovery position, 999 if over 5 minutes). For SCA: AED on site and accessible, staff CPR-trained, Emergency Action Plan with named personnel and communication plan, screening of performers. At least one contrast — e.g. having equipment and plans is essential but only effective if staff are trained and confident to use them.
Secure (3–4 marks): Measures for both conditions described with some explanation.
Developing (2 marks): One condition covered adequately, the other only briefly.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant safety measure. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Every year, young athletes suffer sudden cardiac arrest during sport. Many do not survive because bystanders do not act quickly enough or the right equipment is not available.

Evaluate the extent to which having trained staff and defibrillators at all sporting venues would reduce deaths from sudden cardiac arrest in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that trained staff and on-site AEDs significantly improve survival rates (evidence: survival rates can exceed 70% when CPR and defibrillation are started within 3–5 minutes, compared to less than 10% when emergency services arrive first). Counter-arguments should include: cost and maintenance of AEDs, need for regular retraining, the fact that most cardiac arrests still occur without warning despite screening, and that lifestyle changes and pre-participation screening may be more preventive. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about the relative importance of different strategies.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides explored with some application; partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists benefits without counter-argument or clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes a symptom of an epileptic seizure affecting the limbs?
What is the correct compression-to-breath ratio when performing CPR on an adult?
During sudden cardiac arrest, the performer is unconscious and has _____, which means the heart is no longer pumping blood effectively.
options: breathing difficulties or no normal breathing

knowledge_checks.q: Anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) work by _____ the brain's electrical activity to reduce the frequency and severity of seizures.
Match each condition to its key distinguishing feature.
right: Recurring seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain
Blocked coronary artery; heart continues to beat; performer remains conscious
Electrical failure of the heart; performer unconscious and not breathing normally

flashcard_questions.a: A neurological condition in which abnormal electrical activity in the brain causes recurrent seizures affecting movement, sensation or consciousness.

flashcard_questions.q: State three triggers for epileptic seizures relevant to sport.
flashcard_questions.a: Severe head injuries, anxiety or stress, and tiredness or lack of sleep are the three specification triggers for epileptic seizures.

flashcard_questions.q: Describe one symptom of a seizure affecting the eyes.
flashcard_questions.a: During a seizure the eyes may stare blankly or show fluttering or flickering of the eyelids, which can be mistaken for a brief absence.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the ketogenic diet and how does it help epilepsy?
flashcard_questions.a: A high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet that reduces seizure frequency in some patients, particularly children, when medication is not fully effective.
SCA is caused by an electrical malfunction in the heart, which may be triggered by underlying genetic heart conditions, intense physical activity or sudden trauma.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between a heart attack and sudden cardiac arrest?
flashcard_questions.a: A heart attack blocks a coronary artery but the heart keeps beating and the person stays conscious; cardiac arrest stops the heart entirely, causing unconsciousness.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an AED (Automated External Defibrillator) do?
flashcard_questions.a: An AED analyses the heart's rhythm and delivers a controlled electric shock to restore a normal rhythm if ventricular fibrillation is detected.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the CPR compression-to-breath ratio and rate for an adult in cardiac arrest?
flashcard_questions.a: 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths, delivered at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute, pushing 5 to 6 cm deep.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does every minute without defibrillation matter in SCA?
flashcard_questions.a: Every minute without defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by approximately 10%, making fast action with an AED critical.

flashcard_questions.q: What should a first aider do if an epileptic seizure lasts more than 5 minutes?
flashcard_questions.a: Call 999 immediately, as a prolonged seizure (status epilepticus) is a medical emergency requiring urgent paramedic intervention.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two symptoms of sudden cardiac arrest.
flashcard_questions.a: The two specification symptoms of SCA are unconsciousness (sudden collapse with no response) and breathing difficulties or absence of normal breathing.

flashcard_questions.q: What lifestyle changes can reduce the long-term risk of cardiac arrest?
flashcard_questions.a: Maintaining a healthy weight, not smoking and taking regular cardiovascular exercise all reduce the risk of cardiac events over time.
